title: My first week at a new job
text:
Last Monday I started a new job at a small software company. The office is near the river, so I go there by bike every morning. On my first day, my manager, Linh, showed me the building and introduced me to the team. There are six people in my team: four developers, one designer and one tester.

On Tuesday I got a laptop and an account for the company chat. I read a lot of documents and asked many questions. Everyone was patient and friendly. On Wednesday I fixed my first small bug. It was only one line of code, but I was very happy.

We have a short meeting every morning at nine o'clock. Each person says what they did yesterday and what they will do today. At first I was nervous about speaking English in the meeting, but now it is easier. Next week I will start working on a new feature.

title: A Saturday at the market
text:
Every Saturday morning, Minh and his sister go to the market near their home. They usually leave the house at seven o'clock, because the vegetables are fresh and the market is not crowded yet.

Minh likes to buy fruit. This week he bought mangoes, bananas and a big watermelon. His sister prefers vegetables and fish. She always talks with the sellers and asks about the price before she buys anything. Sometimes she gets a small discount.

After shopping, they sit at a small café at the corner of the market. Minh drinks iced coffee and his sister drinks tea. They talk about their week and plan meals for the next few days. Then they carry their heavy bags home. Minh says the market is more fun than the supermarket because it is full of people, colors and noise.

title: How to run a better online meeting
text:
Many teams now spend hours every week in online meetings, but a lot of that time is wasted. A few simple habits can make meetings shorter and more useful.

First, send an agenda before the meeting. When people know the topics in advance, they can prepare and the discussion stays focused. Second, start on time, even if someone is late. Waiting for latecomers teaches everyone that the start time is not important.

During the meeting, ask people to keep their cameras on if possible. Seeing faces makes it easier to notice when someone is confused or wants to speak. It also helps to choose one person to take notes and write down every decision and action item, with a name and a deadline next to each one.

Finally, end the meeting a few minutes early. This gives people a short break before their next call. After the meeting, share the notes within an hour, while everyone still remembers what was decided.

title: Why sleep matters for learning
text:
When we want to learn something quickly, the first thing many of us cut is sleep. We stay up late to finish a course or review vocabulary. However, research suggests that this is often a mistake.

While we sleep, the brain does not simply rest. It replays what we experienced during the day and moves important information into long-term memory. Students who sleep well after studying usually remember more the next day than students who stay awake for the same number of hours.

Sleep also affects attention. After a short night, it is harder to concentrate, and we make more careless mistakes. For language learners, this means that a tired brain notices fewer details, such as word endings or small differences in pronunciation.

The practical advice is simple: study a little every day, review new words in the evening, and then go to bed at a regular time. Fifteen minutes of practice followed by a good night's sleep can be worth more than an hour of tired study.

title: What we learned from a payment outage
text:
Last month our payment service was unavailable for forty minutes during the evening peak. Around twelve percent of checkout attempts failed, and our support team received more than three hundred messages from frustrated customers.

The root cause turned out to be surprisingly ordinary. A configuration change reduced the size of the database connection pool, and nobody noticed because the change looked harmless in review. When traffic grew in the evening, requests began to wait for free connections, timed out, and were retried by the mobile app, which only made the queue longer.

We have since made three changes. Configuration is now validated by automated checks, so a pool size below a safe minimum fails the build. The mobile app retries with exponential backoff instead of immediately. Most importantly, we added an alert on checkout error rate, which would have woken us up within two minutes instead of the twenty it actually took.

No single person caused the outage, and we deliberately avoided looking for someone to blame. The goal of a post-mortem is to make the system safer, not to punish the people who operate it.

title: Saying no without damaging the relationship
text:
Most professionals know the feeling: a colleague or client asks for something reasonable, but you simply do not have the time. Saying yes to everything leads to missed deadlines and burnout, yet a blunt no can damage a relationship you have spent years building.

Negotiation experts suggest a different approach. Instead of answering immediately, acknowledge the request and show that you understand why it matters. Then explain your current priorities honestly, and offer an alternative: a later date, a smaller version of the task, or a colleague who might be better placed to help.

For example, rather than saying "I can't do this," you might say, "I can see why this report is urgent. I'm committed to the release until Thursday, but I could prepare a short summary by Friday, or ask Nam whether he has time today."

This kind of answer protects your focus while keeping the conversation constructive. The other person leaves with a realistic plan instead of a refusal, and you are more likely to be trusted the next time you do say yes.

title: The quiet cost of AI shortcuts
text:
AI assistants have made it remarkably easy to produce a first draft of almost anything: an email, a test suite, a project proposal. For experienced professionals, this is a genuine gift, since the tedious part of the work shrinks while judgment remains firmly in human hands.

The picture is less straightforward for people who are still building their expertise. Skills such as structuring an argument or debugging an unfamiliar system are acquired precisely through the struggle that these tools remove. A junior developer who accepts generated code without fully understanding it may ship features faster in the short term, yet find themselves unable to reason about the system when something breaks in production.

None of this is an argument for abandoning the tools. It is, however, a case for using them deliberately. One effective practice is to attempt a problem unaided for a fixed period before consulting an assistant, and then to compare the two solutions critically. Another is to ask the tool to explain its reasoning, treating its answer as a hypothesis to be verified rather than an authority to be trusted.

Organizations have a role to play as well. Teams that reward only speed will inevitably encourage shortcuts; those that also value understanding, through code reviews that ask why rather than merely what, are likely to develop more resilient engineers.

title: Deep work in a distracted office
text:
Open-plan offices and instant messaging were intended to make collaboration effortless, and in many respects they have succeeded. Questions are answered in seconds, and decisions no longer wait for the next scheduled meeting. The hidden price, however, is fragmented attention.

Studies of knowledge workers consistently find that after an interruption it can take well over ten minutes to return fully to a complex task. Since many people are interrupted every few minutes, a significant share of the working day may be spent recovering focus rather than using it. Unsurprisingly, the work that suffers most is precisely the kind that demands sustained concentration: designing systems, writing carefully, or solving problems nobody has solved before.

Some teams have responded by negotiating explicit agreements about availability. Mornings might be reserved for uninterrupted work, with notifications muted and meetings forbidden, while afternoons are left open for discussion. Others rely on asynchronous habits, such as writing questions in a shared document that colleagues answer when they reach a natural pause.

Such arrangements require trust, because they make people temporarily unreachable. Yet the teams that adopt them often report not only better output but also lower stress, suggesting that constant availability was never as essential as it seemed.
